notation.meaning: Unemployed and employed workers in period $t$
Separation rate: share of employed workers who lose their job each period
Unemployment rate $U/L$ and its steady state
Matching efficiency, tightness and matching elasticity, when $f$ comes from a matching function

blocks.md: Think of unemployment as water in a bathtub. Each month some employed people lose or leave their jobs and pour in; some unemployed people find jobs and drain out. If more pours in than drains out, the tub fills; if less, it empties. The level settles where the two flows are equal. That settled level is the steady-state unemployment rate. It is high when jobs end often and low when the unemployed find work quickly. Nothing about it requires the labor market to "clear": people are always moving through unemployment, even when the rate itself stays put.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: It turns two measurable flow rates into the unemployment rate, so any policy or shock can be read through what it does to separations or to job finding.
With a labor force $L = U + E$, a separation rate $\lambda$ and a job-finding rate $f$, unemployment evolves as
It is constant when inflows equal outflows, $\lambda\bar{E} = f\bar{U}$, which gives
Substitute $\bar{E} = L - \bar{U}$ into $\lambda\bar{E} = f\bar{U}$ and divide by $L$: $\lambda(1 - \bar{u}) = f\bar{u}$, so $\bar{u}(\lambda + f) = \lambda$.

$\lambda = 0.03$ a month and $f = 0.40$: $\bar{u} = 0.03/0.43 = 7.0\%$. A worker who loses a job expects to stay unemployed $1/f = 2.5$ months; a job lasts $1/\lambda \approx 33$ months on average. Raising $f$ to 0.50 lowers $\bar{u}$ to 5.7%.

| Change | Effect on $\bar{u}$ |
| --- | --- |
| Separation rate $\lambda$ ↑ | ↑ |
| Job-finding rate $f$ ↑ | ↓ |

When $f$ comes from a [Matching Function](note:matching-function), $f = A\theta^{1-\alpha}$, so higher matching efficiency or a tighter market lowers $\bar{u}$; the resulting downward-sloping relation between vacancies and unemployment is the [Beveridge Curve](note:beveridge-curve).

- **Writing $\bar{u} = \lambda/f$.** That is the ratio of unemployed to *employed*, $\bar{U}/\bar{E}$, not to the labor force.
- **Reading a constant $\bar{u}$ as no movement.** Flows continue; only the stock is constant.
- Labor macroeconomics: decomposing unemployment changes into separations and job finding; the steady-state block of the [Diamond-Mortensen-Pissarides Model](note:diamond-mortensen-pissarides-model).
